subject: frostAxe
pitch:
Category: Fantasy weapon.
Subject: frost-forged battle axe.
Style: League of Legends.
reasoning:
I'm planning a TypeScript module for a frost-forged battle axe prop with a League of Legends-style icy blue/silver aesthetic, considering whether a minimal root joint is needed even though it's a weapon rather than a creature.

Now I'm designing the physical layout: a vertical axe planted into a small frozen stone/ice-shard base, with an ornate asymmetric double-head — a large crescent blade with crystal inlay on one side and a smaller spiked ice-fang on the other, plus a glowing crystal at the center of the head. I'm working out orientation (blade plane in XY, thickness along Z) and extrusion approach for the outline geometry.

I'm then planning the base plinth proportions relative to the head span, and starting on the haft — a tapered metallic sweep with banded wraps, sized to run from the base up to the head.

For the wraps I'll use clusters of thin rings around the grip section rather than a continuous mesh, keeping the part count efficient, and I'll apply a gradient paint along the haft transitioning toward frosted tones near the top.

Now I'm working out the head geometry — placing it near the top of the haft with a spike above it, and sketching the crescent blade outline as a series of coordinate points relative to the socket center.

I'm weighing whether the outer blade edge should curve inward or bulge outward like the big Freljord-style axes, leaning toward a convex sweep with notched inner cuts for a more dramatic silhouette.

Still plotting blade points...

Now working on the mirrored spike shape for the opposite side, sketching a thinner fang-like curve that sweeps outward and upward.

Next I'm layering the blade: a base ice-steel slab plus a smaller inset plate scaled inward at a raised z-height for a bright icy glow, with the cutting edge made especially luminous.

I'm also planning a decal layer—a frost fern or rune pattern rendered on a plane with transparent cutouts, placed just above the blade surface on both front and back faces for a glowing etched effect.

I'm shading the blade faces with a gradient from dark blue near the socket to icy white at the edge, with bright white highlights on the beveled walls, and adding a thinner inner plate scaled down and offset for a layered look.

Now I'm setting thickness values for the main blade versus the inner plate, giving the plate a darker navy etched tone so the edges stay bright and create a two-tone raised panel effect, plus a thin glow decal plane positioned just above it. I'm also thinking through the central head hub where the blade meets the haft — a silver steel collar with deep blue and cyan glow accents, maybe gold trim, fitting the Freljord frost aesthetic.

Settling on a palette: light steel, mid steel, navy, deep navy, ice cyan, glow white, pale gold trim, and off-white fur tone for a wrap near the head. I'm picturing fur tufts scattered along a swept haft surface for that Freljord touch, then moving on to design a large central crystal set into the front and back of the head.

Planning a stretched octahedron crystal in glowing cyan framed by a ringed lathe shape, with smaller frost-shard crystals as translucent-glow cones along the blade and horn tips. Then I'm sketching the hub as a dark navy box with trim, topped by a spiked cap, pushing the total weapon height toward two meters with a hero-scaled head around 1.35 wide.

Working through the base proportions -- widening the base radius slightly to 0.55 so it comfortably supports the asymmetric head footprint, and centering the haft at x=0 so the head extends unevenly from -0.7 to 0.65. Now I'm planning how the haft sinks into the base, with a ferrule band and cone near the bottom, plus a small crack detail to sell the planted-axe look.

I'm adding frost crystals clustering around the planting point, then sweeping the haft geometry through a path of points with a radius profile that gives it a subtle grip swell, using flat faceted sides rather than smooth shading.

For the leather wrap I'm using a spiral sweep around the grip between the mid and upper sections, defining the center axis, turns, pitch, and radius so it winds naturally up the handle, then coloring it as leather. Next I'm planning torus or lathe rings as decorative bands at a few key heights along the haft.

Then I'm orienting small torus rings as metal band accents aligned along the Y axis at a couple positions near the top, and considering whether to add a fur collar ring of outward-facing cards just below the head for texture.

I'm also thinking about hanging fur using two rings at slightly different heights with downward flow and spin variation, plus a tufted fur texture in white-blue gradient. Beyond that, I want a hanging cloth banner or pennant near the head — a thin swallowtail flag attached to the front of the haft with rune and gold trim details.

Now I'm working out the ribbon tails hanging from the collar, one front and one back, each a thin swallowtail-shaped extrusion facing forward, defining their outline points and proportions to get a natural draped look.

I'll paint them navy with gold border stripes based on proximity to the edges, and skip extra rune decals for now to keep things simple. Then I start assembling the hub at the head center with a navy-steel box for the core structure.

Still shaping the spearhead geometry...

Checking the tip heights — the spear reaches about 2.02 while the pick's tip is taller at roughly 2.12, so I need to reconcile those proportions.

I'm resetting the head center to y=1.3, adjusting the pick tip to 2.04 and the spear tip to 2.0 so they align better, then working out the hub box dimensions and socket placement before moving on to the gusset plates connecting the blades to the hub.

Shaping the kite-outline hub and gold trim sweep...

For the hero element, I'm now thinking about a central crystal that pokes through the hub on both faces—an elongated octahedron scaled to protrude slightly past each side, positioned at the hub's center.

I'm adding gold torus ring frames as bezels around the crystal on each face, plus planning how the blade pairs will slot into the hub's thickness and sketching icy frost spikes as small cones along the blade's top edge.

I'm defining a helper function to generate each shard with its glow color, then planning frost shards along the bottom edge pointing downward, plus runes and a fern-like glowing decal texture for the main blade.

Now I'm sizing and positioning the frost crystal texture plane to overlay the inner blade plate, sketching a central line with angled branches radiating outward while keeping within the plate bounds.

For the back face, I'm considering how mirroring affects the drawing—since viewing from behind flips left-right, hub-side orientation would swap. I'll likely just design the frost pattern as roughly symmetric so the mirror issue doesn't matter, avoiding the need for separate UV flipping or duplicate textures.

Working through this, right is -X, confirming local +X maps to viewer's right, so the back plane needs flipped UVs to get the tip on the correct side. I apply the same mirroring logic to the pick position on the -X side for the front view.

So flip condition works out to zSign*s<0 — front with s=+1 unflipped, s=-1 flipped, and back inverted accordingly. I'm also noting that glow materials clone from the part's base material so the textured color still comes through, and now I'm turning to the edge highlight paint for the main blade, where the outline coordinates are in meters relative to the extrude, not the model.

For the wall faces, the normal direction comes from crossing the local x and y basis vectors, giving a clean z-aligned normal scaled by the side sign, so checking its absolute z component lets me pick out near-vertical walls for a bright rim. I'm blending navy-steel to frost based on a smoothstep across the outline's x position, then adding a frost noise overlay for texture. For the beveled edges, since the normal sweeps through a quarter circle, I'm loosening the rim threshold so the whole bevel reads as a bright highlighted edge.

Now I'm planning the inner plate: deep navy etched with frost-blue noise, plus small gold rivet studs near the hub rendered as tiny spheres, and maybe glowing cyan octahedron gems set into the plate's corners as decorative sockets. For the base, I'm sketching a lathed octagonal stone plinth profile with a flat-shaded low-poly look, using mottled navy-gray stone coloring.

Continuing that, I'm adding a snow cap on top of the plinth with a paint function that switches between snow-white and stone color based on surface normal, topping it with a squashed-sphere snow mound. I'm also scattering an irregular ring of upward-angled ice shards around the base (keeping the front view clear with smaller shards there), plus a glowing rune-inscribed decal ring flush on the plinth's top surface.

Writing rune ring SVG...

I'm scattering ice-shards around the base at eight positions, tilting them outward with varied heights, keeping the front-facing ones smaller so the pitch stays visible. I'm also adding a few icicles hanging down from the blade's inner edge for extra frost detail, plus considering a fur-tuft texture card for a collar.

For the collar, I'll use a small torus shape as a thick ring base, colored white-blue like fur, positioned just under the hub with cards wrapped around it at slightly varying radii to suggest fur depth. Then I'm adding hanging ribbons offset to the sides so they don't overlap the fur cards, draping down over the lower body.

I'm trying to find a spot for the ribbons hanging below the spearhead near the hub, avoiding collision with the crystal and blades. I'll simplify by shrinking the fur cards and placing the ribbons just outside the torus so they overlap the tuft slightly rather than getting buried.

Instead, I'll attach the ribbons to a gold ring around the haft below the fur, letting them hang from a knotted point near the grip wrap, nudging the z-offset outward so they clear the wrap's radius without clipping.

Now I'm mapping out the full haft layout: ferrule cone from 0.17-0.34, grip wrap 0.40-0.85 with bands at 0.38 and 0.87, a gold tie ring at 0.88 with ribbons hanging down to 0.50, and a fur collar around 0.9-1.06 touching the gold band near the hub bottom at 1.09. I'm settling on a dark blue-steel grain for the haft color.

I'm shaping the ferrule with a lathe profile extending from 0.17 to 0.33, giving it a frost-forged steel look with white paint near the edges and subtle glowing cyan veins. Now I'm planning out the texture set (targeting 5-12 total): frost blade, pick rune, rune ring base, fur tuft, and deciding whether to add snow particles or skip them.

For the remaining textures, I'm adding a crest emblem on the hub, a rune glowing on the ribbon, and floating frost sparkle cards scattered around the axe (~14 instances) using star-shaped glowing textures placed on upward-facing frames.

I'm skipping extra snow frosting on the blade top, but adding a thin pale gold trim sweep along the hub kite outline and rivets for a finishing detail.

I'm also considering a subtle edge glint — a thin cyan-glow sweep along the main blade's outer edge points, offset slightly inward so it reads as a highlight rather than overlapping the painted edge bevel.

Writing sweep code...

I'll keep everything attached to the root joint to avoid bone assignment complications, skipping extra joints like an axe-specific one. For parts, I'm defining a signature with position, direction, axis, rotation, scale, texture, and bone options, plus a flat-shading flag, and writing a helper function to generate elongated shard shapes based on direction vectors and length/radius parameters.

Now I'm figuring out how to build crystal shapes — combining a hexagonal prism body with a pointed cone tip, using cone geometry so the tip naturally points along the given direction.

I'm deciding whether to glow all the crystal facets or not — full emissive glow flattens the faceted shading, so I'll keep most shards non-glow with pale icy colors to preserve the faceted look, and reserve the glow effect for just the main crystal, rune decals, edges, sparkles, and gems.

Now I'm writing the SVG for the rune ring, generating runes in a loop around the circle...

Adding branch strokes and highlight details...

Now sketching the pick's decorative texture, placing small diamond rune marks along its diagonal within a scaled inset plate.

Working through the centerline geometry between the upper and lower edges of the blade, I'm tracing the midpoints to estimate a slope around 0.85, then placing the plane center near (0.32, 0.24) along that diagonal.

I'll skip the inner plate and keep the pick simple with a glowing spine line and rim paint. For the ribbon, I'm adding a small rune texture plane with gold borders, plus a four-pointed sparkle star SVG for extra decal detail.

Now I'm deciding where to place an emblem — maybe a frost sigil plaque on the plinth's front face, since the hub area is already crowded with the crystal.

I'll add a frost crack decal near the plant point, placed slightly below the rune ring to avoid z-fighting, giving 7 textures total. Then I'll paint the base top with snow-blue mottling blended by normal direction, and keep the lathe profile spun 22.5° so a flat face centers front.

Fixing base profile...

I'm checking the rune ring radius fits within the plane bounds, then planning rocky bulges and snow caps around the edges—icosahedron rocks sunk at the rear half, with larger ice crystal clusters framing back-left and back-right while keeping the front low. Now I'm starting to write the full implementation code.

Setting up imports and color palette...

Still writing blade shading...

Now I'm writing a flat gold paint and a blade-builder function that extrudes an outline into a 3D shape with thickness, bevel, and color. I'm also working out the right TypeScript type for outline points, deciding whether to import the OutlinePoint type or just define my own tuple type locally to avoid mismatches.

Writing scaling function...

I'm checking that the scaled inner plate stays non-crossing and looks like a ridge near the hub, then adjusting to non-uniform scaling factors for a nicer proportion. I'm also planning gem placements, moving them off the main body onto the plate near the hub, symmetric top and bottom.

Writing decal plane helper...

Checking the flip logic for the s=-1 mirrored side: the texture was drawn assuming hub-on-left from the viewer's perspective, so I need to verify when zs*s is negative that flip should trigger, confirming the picked orientation matches hub-left for that side.

For the glow pass I'm reusing the material's existing map as the emissive map so the texture itself glows, keeping alpha test intact and tinting with white. Now I'm defining the hub shape as an octagonal kite outline and extruding it into a small beveled 3D piece centered at the frame, assigning it the hub color.

Next I'm adding a decorative gold trim sweep around a slightly inset version of that outline on both faces, then moving on to lathe-built collar rings for the top and bottom sockets near the hub, starting with the profile for the upper socket.

Still defining the haft sweep... and now adding a spiral wrap around the shaft using a helical sweep with small radius to simulate wound cord.

Then I'm placing torus rings as decorative bands at a few heights along the haft, orienting the torus axis to align with the grip's length, plus gold studs at the grip ends and a lathed ferrule near the base.

Adding fur collar rings around y=1.0 using the ring helper with counts and radii, and scattering small card-shaped leaf elements with lean, flow, and bend parameters for natural variation, leaving their color to default from the texture rather than tinting them.

Now working out the ribbon geometry — placing a gold tie band torus at y=0.88 with ribbon strips extruded downward over the wrap region, front and back pieces offset slightly in z with small thickness for depth.

I'm writing the ribbon's coloring logic: a paint function that checks local coordinates to color the border gold near the edges, adds a subtle striped pattern, and blends two blue tones elsewhere for the cloth-like fabric look.

Now I'm placing a rune texture plane onto the ribbon's front and back faces, positioning it just above the thickness offset, and adding a slight bevel to the ribbon's edge geometry. I'm moving on to building the spear: setting up the socket, blade shape, and a glowing fuller down the blade's center using an extruded outline positioned above the shaft.

Defining spear outline points...

I'm now sketching frosty crystal shards sprouting from the blade's top inner notch, giving directions and lengths for each shard cluster.

Adjusting the pick's tip height so it clears the spear tip, then setting up a mirrored helper function to place shards along the pick's upper edge based on a scale factor, position, and direction—followed by starting on the central hub crystal as an octahedron shape.

Good, torus already lies flat in the XY plane so no direction override needed. I'm adding small gold rivet spheres at the blade-hub joints on front and back corners, and sketching a stone paint function that shades snowy highlights near the top of the normal and blends cooler tones below.

Now I'm placing scattered rock formations around the base at various angles with radius 0.5, using scaled icosahedron geometry for a jagged look, colored with the stone shader, and adding snow caps on top of each rock.

For the crystal clusters, I'm setting up a random generator to position groups of three tilted crystals outward from the base at different angles and scales, computing each one's direction and length procedurally.

Still writing crystal geometry...

Now I'm planning the crystal color palette and the layout of sparkle elements scattered around the head region.

Checking that the crack plane's orientation reads upright to the viewer, and confirming no z-fighting between the decal planes and the lathe top or haft/ferrule placement. Now sketching the frost crack as a jagged radial SVG pattern of zigzag rays from center.

Finalizing minor extras — skipping additional embellishments like snow caps, extra gems, or hanging charms since the shard and crack details are sufficient — then moving to tally the overall part count for the build.

I'll place four edge positions with outward normals, duplicating each as a tilted pair along z to form a little frost crown along the blade. That rounds out the seven textures — blade frost, pick rune, rune ring, crack, ribbon rune, star, fur — so now I'm moving on to writing the actual SVG generator code.

Writing frost branch paths...

Still writing branch coordinates...

I'm clamping the branch positions to stay within bounds, then checking how the plane shape should fit relative to the inner plate's coordinate region.

I should check whether decal lines could float beyond the plate edge into empty air, but the fern pattern only spans about ±0.17 around center, well inside the blade's ±0.4 extent, so it's safely contained. Since it looks small relative to the blade, I'll bump up the scale so the fern spans closer to ±0.25, adjusting the SVG height and point range accordingly.

Now I'm setting the plane dimensions and center offset, defining a point type that allows marking sharp corners, and working out the extrude settings—picking a tapered thickness that's thicker near the hub and thinner toward the tip, with a small bevel. I'm deciding the scatter/surface decoration isn't needed here, just sticking with the core extrude and card-based approach to keep things simple.

Now I'm setting up the builder with a root joint and considering whether to add a separate head joint along the haft for the axe head parts, but deciding to keep the rig simple and let nearest-joint logic handle part assignment instead of being fully explicit. I'm also planning deterministic sparkle positions using a seeded random generator.

Writing sparkle SVG and fur tuft shapes...

Defining rune glyph shapes and placing twelve of them radially around a circle with rotation transforms...

I'm also adding concentric circles with tick marks for the dial, scaling the whole ring to physical units so the strokes read cleanly at render resolution. Now I'm moving to the overall scene assembly, deciding which geometries should use flat vs smooth shading, and laying out the positions of the base rocks around the scene using angular offsets from the vertical axis.

Placing the sparkle particles next, scattering them within a radius and height range around the frame. Writing the main blade extrusion with its thickness and bevel parameters...

Pruning unused imports and defining the leather, haft, and hub paint functions with mixed color noise and grain textures for each material.

Working out gem placement on the plate (octahedron shapes, scaled and glowing) and double-checking the ring helper's return shape before finalizing the code.
